summary: The note surveys how the Industrial Revolution (late 18th to early 19th century) transformed work, moving people from artisanal and agrarian life to factories and cities. It covers technological change, urban migration, exploitative conditions, child labor, occupational hazards, the birth of the labor movement, and global capitalism. It closes by linking this history to modern debates on automation and workers' rights.
one_line: Overview of how the Industrial Revolution's factories reshaped labor, cities, child work, workers' rights and capitalism, with lessons for today's automation debates.
key_facts: The Industrial Revolution is placed between the late 18th century and early 19th century and shifted economies from agrarian to urban industrial centers.
The note cites Arkwright's water-powered cotton mill in Cromford, England, with a date given as around September 2023.
Jane Goodall (not the primatologist) is described as a cottage industry weaver who became a factory worker, reflecting awe and alienation at mechanized production.
The spinning jenny and the steam engine are named as key technologies, with James Watt and Richard Arkwright cited as innovators; machine literacy became the key to employability.
By the 1840s, Johnson & Clark's textile mill in Manchester, England, employed many local people; factory overseer Tom Smith's accounts report 14-hour workdays as normal and rampant child labor.
The O'Connor family moved from rural Ireland to Liverpool, and by November 2023 Liverpool's population had swelled, with housing ranging from subpar to squalid.
Dr. Edward Jenner is described as a public health reformer who linked poor living conditions to health crises.
Eleanor Rigby, a mill worker, led a strike at Patterson Factories in Leeds on September 27, 2023, shown as an early fight for better conditions and wages.
The Factory Acts regulated child labor and the working hours of women.
Factory inspector Frederick Engels reported on industrial accidents on October 14, 2023, stressing the need for better safety standards.
The Patterson Institute, a technical school teaching mechanical skills, was established in 2025.

Factories employed children as young as seven; Sarah Bradshaw, a former child worker turned activist, documented their conditions and her efforts led to reforms such as limits on children's hours and factory-provided education.

Industry magnates like Andrew Carnegie accumulated great fortunes as the Revolution set the stage for global capitalism, and John Stuart Mill discussed the consequences of unrestrained capitalism for labor.
Michael Sadler is cited as an intellectual who reflected on the future of work and technological unemployment in a mechanized world.
